passage: Yash arrived early at the regional office's monthly review, as he always did, to have a word with the branch head over tea. He asked about her daughter's exam, remembered her dog's name and made sure she knew his team had cleared the audit early. That part was just being warm and useful. Then Ayesha's loan report came up. Yash knew the gaps came from a mistake in his own department's file, and said only, “I did notice a few gaps in it,” and watched the head's eyebrows rise. The two other managers nodded along. A junior analyst studied a pen. Ayesha looked at the page, then at Yash, who reached for his tea and found the cup unusually heavy.

qa.q: What did Yash ask the branch head about over tea?
qa.a: Yash asked about her daughter's exam.

qa.q: What might Yash have been feeling when the cup seemed unusually heavy?
qa.a: Yash seems uneasy or guilty, since he knew the gaps came from a mistake in his own department's file and let Ayesha take the blame.

qa.q: What could Yash do next to keep his ambition without harming Ayesha?
qa.a: Yash could tell the branch head the real source of the gaps and keep building his reputation through the honest parts, like the early audit.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt as Ayesha looked at Yash?
qa.a: Ayesha may have felt blindsided and puzzled, since the report was being marked down in front of the room by someone who knew more.

grounding: An ambitious employee networks normally and then lets someone else absorb the blame, showing where influence turns into undermining and hiding facts.

passage:
Subject: Need to think aloud
Dear Mridul,
Since college you've been the person I can be honest with, so here it is. Since I joined the sales team I've been building relationships on purpose: coffee with the regional director, remembering names, sharing credit with people who matter. I don't think that's wrong. Last week, though, I held back a customer-complaint figure that would have helped Farah, who sits opposite, in her presentation, because it made my own numbers look better beside hers. Nobody knows. The whole team clapped for me, and Farah congratulated me first. I keep replaying it. I want to rise, but I'm not sure I want to rise like this.
Mohit

qa.q: What kind of figure did Mohit hold back?
qa.a: Mohit held back a customer-complaint figure.

qa.q: Why does Mohit keep replaying the moment when Farah congratulated Mohit first?
qa.a: Mohit feels uneasy about the hidden figure, since Farah's warmth makes the omission sting, though Mohit still wants to rise.

qa.q: What could Mohit do about the held-back figure?
qa.a: Mohit could share the figure with Farah and the team now, and keep the ordinary relationship-building that is not harmful.

qa.q: How might Farah see the presentation if Farah later learns about the figure?
qa.a: Farah might feel hurt and doubt Mohit's warmth, since the missing figure would have helped and the congratulations came first.

grounding: An ambitious employee builds alliances, which is normal, but holds back a fact that would have helped Farah, which is where it turns harmful.

passage: First week of April: Bidisha, new to the marketing team, started having lunch with people from sales and finance. She asked about their targets and remembered their children's names. It was friendly and useful. Mid-April: the promotion list was coming. When Nazia's campaign numbers came in low, Bidisha mentioned it to the director over coffee, 'just so you're not surprised', but left out that the budget had been cut halfway. She felt a small rush, and then a small knot in her stomach. End of May: the director praised Bidisha in the team meeting. Nazia sat three seats away, not looking up. Later, a finance colleague mentioned the budget cut in passing, and the director turned to look at Bidisha for a long moment.

qa.q: What did Bidisha leave out when mentioning Nazia's numbers?
qa.a: That the budget had been cut halfway.

qa.q: What did Bidisha feel after the coffee with the director?
qa.a: A small rush of excitement, followed by a knot of guilt in her stomach.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha cross from normal networking into harm, and what could she have done instead?
qa.a: When she hid the budget cut to make Nazia look bad; she could have kept building contacts honestly and let her own work speak.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia in the May meeting?
qa.a: Nazia sits not looking up while Bidisha is praised, likely feeling hurt and undermined.

grounding: Over two months an ambitious employee moves from normal networking to shaping impressions by hiding facts, with consequences.

passage: Rashmi, you're asking how to get noticed? Sit, and let old Rukmini tell you something. In 1998 I was a sharp young officer at the textile corporation, hungry to rise. I made friends in every department. I remembered birthdays, I carried sweets to the accounts section. That was fine; people liked me, and I liked them. But when the deputy manager post opened, I went further. My colleague Suresh had made a costing error, and he fixed it in time. I made sure the general manager heard about the error and not the fix. I got the post. Suresh stopped greeting me. Later the general manager learned the full story and never trusted me with anything important again. Build friendships, child. Just don't build them on someone else's back.

qa.q: What did Suresh do after making the costing error?
qa.a: He fixed it in time.

qa.q: What might Suresh have felt when he stopped greeting Rukmini?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt betrayed and angry that Rukmini had told only half the story to win the post.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned Rukmini's networking harmful?
qa.a: Making sure the general manager heard about Suresh's error but not the fix; the friendships were fine, but hiding facts to undermine Suresh was not.

qa.q: How did the general manager see Rukmini after learning the full story?
qa.a: The general manager stopped trusting Rukmini with anything important, seeing the promotion as unfairly won.

grounding: A senior recalls how friendly networking was fine until hiding a colleague's fix to rise cost lasting trust.

passage: The audit was at nine the next morning, the office air-conditioning had failed, and half the team had gone home sweaty and grumpy. Wasim stayed, partly to finish and partly because he knew the regional manager, Mr Bakshi, noticed who stayed. He brought Mr Bakshi tea and chatted about cricket; that part felt fine. Then, checking the shared folder, he spotted a wrong total in Tanvir's section. Tanvir was his main rival for team lead. It would be easy to say nothing and let the auditors find it, or to mention it to Mr Bakshi now, casually, as Tanvir's carelessness. Wasim sat with it in the heat. Then he picked up his phone and messaged Tanvir: 'Row 48 total looks off. Fixing it with a note so you can check.' Tanvir replied with a thumbs-up at 11:40.

qa.q: What did Wasim spot in Tanvir's section?
qa.a: A wrong total, in row 48.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he sat with the error?
qa.a: Wasim felt tempted and torn, seeing an easy way to beat a rival, and uneasy about what that would mean.

qa.q: Which of Wasim's choices were fair networking, and which would have crossed a line?
qa.a: Staying late and chatting with Mr Bakshi is normal; hiding the error or using it to make Tanvir look careless would have undermined a colleague.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel getting the late-night message?
qa.a: Tanvir likely felt relieved and grateful, and may trust Wasim more despite the rivalry.

grounding: Under deadline pressure, an ambitious employee builds goodwill with a manager but stops short of undermining a rival.

passage: Jeevan had worked out the Gurugram office within a month: lunch with the right people, a joke in the regional head's chat, a coffee order remembered. None of it felt wrong. It was just how you got noticed. The trouble started with the client pitch. Deepak had found the costing error that saved it, and at the Friday review everyone turned to him. That night Jeevan drafted a message to the regional head: "Deepak's numbers were a bit shaky earlier, I helped tighten them." It wasn't quite a lie. His thumb hovered over send. He thought of Deepak, who had lent him a charger on his first day, and of Nisha from HR saying, "People here remember who stood on whom." He deleted the second line. Then, slowly, the first.

qa.q: What had Deepak found that saved the client pitch?
qa.a: Deepak had found the costing error that saved it.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as his thumb hovered over send?
qa.a: He was torn and uneasy: ambition pushed him to grab credit, but remembering Deepak's kindness made him hesitate.

qa.q: Where does Jeevan's networking cross a line, and what is fine to keep?
qa.a: Lunches and remembering people's orders are normal; the drafted message undermines Deepak with a half-truth, so deleting it was right.

qa.q: What would change for Deepak if the message had been sent?
qa.a: The regional head might quietly doubt Deepak's work without Deepak ever knowing why, hurting a colleague who had been kind.

grounding: Shows an ambitious employee whose normal networking nearly turns into undermining a colleague, and who pulls back.
